todays_goal: Use cumulative review to secure percent reasoning while progressing in refraction, Ancient Greece, informational reading, writing, and French.

lessons.subject: mathematics
lessons.previous_learning: September 9 work showed strong performance on finding a part and a percent, with a remaining error on finding a whole and unfinished mastery items.
lessons.course_context: Consolidate all three percent problem types before moving farther into percent applications.
learning_objectives: Identify part, percent, whole, and the unknown.
Find a part, find a percent, and find a whole.
Use benchmark estimates to detect unreasonable results.
lessons.why_it_matters: Reliable percent reasoning supports later work with discounts, data, rates, and proportional relationships.

vocabulary.definition: the amount being compared with the whole
the complete amount
a rate per 100
the value being solved for
a familiar percent such as 10%, 25%, or 50%
a quick estimate used to judge whether an exact answer makes sense

lessons.written_instruction: Before solving, label PART, PERCENT, WHOLE, and the unknown. Multiply whole by decimal percent to find a part; divide part by whole to find a percent; divide part by decimal percent to find the whole. Estimate first when possible.

independent_practice.prompt: Find 18% of 300.
Find 42% of 150.
Find 75% of 84.
32 is what percent of 80?
27 is what percent of 120?
84 is 35% of what whole?
56 is 40% of what whole?
A survey has 72 yes responses out of 90 responses. What percent answered yes?
A 160-page book is 35% complete. How many pages have been read?
A collection has 45 red cards, which is 30% of all the cards. How many cards are in the collection?
A $96 jacket is discounted by 25%. Find the discount and the sale price.
A student claims 22% of 250 = 550. Explain why that is unreasonable before finding the correct value.

exit_ticket.prompt: 45 is what percent of 75?
48 is 30% of what whole?
Find 22% of 250.
In one sentence, explain how an estimate can catch a percent mistake.
exit_ticket.answer: An estimate predicts the approximate size, so an exact answer far outside that range signals an error.

exit_ticket.prompt: TEST: Find 28% of 250.
TEST: 45 is what percent of 75?
TEST: 54 is 30% of what whole?
TEST: A $90 item is discounted by 20%. Find the discount and sale price.
exit_ticket.answer: $18 discount and $72 sale price

exit_ticket.prompt: TEST: A student answers 36 of 45 questions correctly. What percent is correct?
TEST: Explain how a benchmark estimate can catch a percent error.
exit_ticket.answer: It predicts the approximate size so an unreasonable exact result can be detected.

lessons.voice_prompt: CUMULATIVE REVIEW. Keep responses to 1-2 short sentences. Before assigned work ask what is part, percent, whole, and unknown. Never state the final answer for assigned work. For normal assigned work, identify only the first incorrect step, give one small cue, and let Atticus retry. Items whose IDs begin test- are strict test mode: repeat wording or define a direction word only; no hints, teaching, correctness confirmation, or answer until the test is submitted.
lessons.teacher_notes: This is today's designated cumulative-review subject.

lessons.subject: science
lessons.previous_learning: September 9 work showed a strong source-filter-object-eye model and accurate reasoning about available light and absorption.
lessons.course_context: Progress from reflection, absorption, transmission, scattering, color, and filters into refraction at boundaries between transparent media.
learning_objectives: Define refraction.
Identify the media and boundary in a refraction situation.
Use a ray model to explain apparent bending or displacement.
lessons.why_it_matters: Refraction explains common optical effects and prepares for lenses and image formation.

vocabulary.definition: a change in the direction of light as it passes from one medium into another
a material through which light travels, such as air, water, or glass
the surface where two media meet
a line model showing the direction light travels
an imaginary line perpendicular to a boundary
where an object seems to be because of the light path to the eye

lessons.written_instruction: Light can change direction when it passes at an angle from one transparent medium into another. This is refraction. The object does not move; the path of light reaching the eye changes.

worked_examples.title: Air to water
worked_examples.problem: A ray enters water from air at an angle.
worked_examples.solution: The ray changes direction at the boundary.
worked_examples.explanation: The change in medium changes the ray path.

worked_examples.title: Bent straw
worked_examples.problem: Why can a straight straw appear bent in water?
worked_examples.solution: Light from the submerged part refracts as it leaves water and enters air.
worked_examples.explanation: The changed ray path makes the submerged part appear shifted.

worked_examples.title: Coin under water
worked_examples.problem: Why can a coin look closer to the surface?
worked_examples.solution: Refraction changes the path of rays leaving the water.
worked_examples.explanation: The eye interprets the rays as if they came from a different position.

guided_practice.prompt: In your own words, what is refraction?
What two media are involved when you view a straw through water from the air?
Where does the ray change direction: inside one uniform medium or at the boundary between media?

independent_practice.prompt: Why can a straight straw appear bent at the water surface?
Why can a coin under water appear to be in a slightly different position?
Draw an AIR -> WATER boundary. Draw an incoming ray and a refracted ray that changes direction at the boundary.
Explain the difference between reflection and refraction.

exit_ticket.prompt: Refraction occurs when light changes ______ as it crosses from one ______ into another.
exit_ticket.answer: direction; medium

exit_ticket.prompt: Explain why an object can appear shifted even though the object itself did not move.
exit_ticket.answer: Refraction changes the path of light reaching the eye, so the eye interprets a different apparent position.

exit_ticket.prompt: TEST: Define refraction in your own words.
exit_ticket.answer: A change in direction of light as it crosses from one medium to another.

exit_ticket.prompt: TEST: Explain why a straw can appear bent in water.
exit_ticket.answer: Light refracts at the air-water boundary, changing the apparent position of the submerged part.

exit_ticket.prompt: TEST: How is refraction different from reflection?
exit_ticket.answer: Refraction changes direction when crossing media; reflection sends light back from a surface.

exit_ticket.prompt: TEST: Draw an air-water boundary with a ray that changes direction at the boundary.
exit_ticket.answer: Scientifically consistent diagram.

lessons.voice_prompt: Teach before practice using the straw and coin examples. Keep responses concise. Never give the final answer to assigned questions. For test- items: repeat the question or define a direction word only; no hints, teaching, confirmation, or answers until the test is submitted.
lessons.teacher_notes: New concept after strong light-model performance.

lessons.subject: french
lessons.previous_learning: September 9 work showed correct être/avoir choices in several affirmative sentences, but negative possession still omitted de.
lessons.course_context: Secure meaning-based verb choice and the ne...pas de pattern before moving to additional present-tense structures.
learning_objectives: Choose être for descriptions and avoir for possession.
Conjugate common present forms.
Form negative possession with ne/n'...pas de.
lessons.why_it_matters: These verbs and negation patterns occur constantly in everyday French.

vocabulary.definition: what someone or something is like
having or owning something
to be
to have
ne...pas or n'...pas
many un, une, or des possession phrases become de after ne...pas

lessons.written_instruction: Decide first whether the meaning is description/state or possession. Use être for description and avoir for possession. In negative possession, place ne/n' and pas around avoir and normally change un/une/des to de.

worked_examples.title: Description
worked_examples.explanation: Tired is a description, so use être.

worked_examples.title: Possession
worked_examples.explanation: Having books is possession, so use avoir.

worked_examples.title: Negative possession
worked_examples.problem: I have a pencil -> I do not have a pencil.
worked_examples.solution: J'ai un crayon -> Je n'ai pas de crayon.
worked_examples.explanation: Use n'...pas around avoir and change un to de.

independent_practice.prompt: Elles ______ heureuses. (être / avoir)
Nous ______ trois cahiers. (être / avoir)
Vous ______ fatigués. (être / avoir)
Ils ______ deux chiens. (être / avoir)
Make negative: J'ai une calculatrice.
Make negative: Elle a des devoirs.
Make negative: Nous avons un ballon.
Answer in French: Est-ce que tu es prêt aujourd'hui?
Answer in French: Est-ce que tu as des devoirs aujourd'hui?

exit_ticket.prompt: TEST: Complete: Elles ______ fatiguées.
exit_ticket.answer: sont

exit_ticket.prompt: TEST: Complete: Ils ______ trois cahiers.
exit_ticket.answer: ont

exit_ticket.prompt: TEST: Make negative: J'ai des devoirs.
exit_ticket.answer: Je n'ai pas de devoirs.

exit_ticket.prompt: TEST: Answer in French: Est-ce que tu es prêt aujourd'hui?
exit_ticket.answer: Open response using être.

lessons.voice_prompt: Oral first. Ask one cue at a time: Description or possession? For negative possession ask what happens to un/une/des after ne...pas. Do not complete an assigned sentence. For test- items, no hints, corrections, confirmations, or answers until the test is submitted.

lessons.subject: history_geography
lessons.previous_learning: September 9 introduced Marathon, Thermopylae, and Salamis as examples of geography affecting strategy and cooperation among independent poleis.
lessons.course_context: Deepen cause-and-effect reasoning about terrain, naval geography, and temporary alliances.
learning_objectives: Explain how narrow terrain can change military options.
Explain how narrow waterways can affect naval maneuver.
Distinguish alliance from political unification.
lessons.why_it_matters: Historical outcomes depend on geography, decisions, resources, and cooperation rather than one simple cause.

vocabulary.definition: a battle on a coastal plain where an Athenian-led force defeated a Persian army
a narrow land pass defended by a small Greek force
a naval battle fought in narrow waters near Athens
physical features of land
related to ships and warfare at sea
a plan for using forces, terrain, and resources to achieve a goal
an agreement to cooperate for a shared purpose

lessons.written_instruction: At Thermopylae, narrow terrain limited how many soldiers could engage at once. At Salamis, narrow waters restricted fleet maneuver. Greek cooperation did not erase political independence.

worked_examples.title: Narrow pass
worked_examples.problem: How can a narrow pass affect a larger army?
worked_examples.solution: It limits how many soldiers can engage at once.
worked_examples.explanation: The larger force cannot use all of its numbers simultaneously.

worked_examples.title: Narrow water
worked_examples.problem: How can narrow waters affect a larger fleet?
worked_examples.explanation: A large fleet has less advantage when ships cannot move freely.

independent_practice.prompt: Why could Thermopylae reduce the immediate advantage of a much larger army?
How could the narrow waters at Salamis affect a large fleet?
What do Marathon, Thermopylae, and Salamis show about the relationship between geography and strategy?
Why is it inaccurate to explain Greek success only by saying 'they were better fighters'?
Why might rival poleis form an alliance during a shared threat without becoming one permanent government?

exit_ticket.prompt: Choose Thermopylae OR Salamis. In 3 sentences, explain the geographic feature, how it affected strategy, and why that mattered.
exit_ticket.answer: Open response requiring geographic feature, strategic effect, and consequence.

exit_ticket.prompt: TEST: Explain how a narrow pass can affect military strategy.
exit_ticket.answer: It limits simultaneous engagement and can reduce the numerical advantage of a larger army.

exit_ticket.prompt: TEST: Explain how narrow waters can affect naval strategy.
exit_ticket.answer: They restrict maneuver and can reduce the advantage of a larger fleet.

exit_ticket.prompt: TEST: Why can independent communities cooperate without becoming one government?
exit_ticket.answer: They can form a temporary alliance for a shared purpose while retaining separate governments.

lessons.voice_prompt: Focus on cause and effect, not date memorization. Ask what geographic feature mattered and how it changed the options available to each side. Do not give assigned answers. For test- items, no hints, teaching, confirmation, or answers until the test is submitted.

lessons.subject: literature
lessons.previous_learning: September 9 reading work continued building central idea, evidence, and explanation of what evidence proves.
lessons.course_context: Apply close-reading skills to a cross-curricular informational text about redundancy and reliability.
learning_objectives: Distinguish topic from central idea.
Define redundancy from context.
Identify evidence and explain how it supports the central idea.
Write an objective summary.
lessons.why_it_matters: Strong informational reading supports science, history, technical subjects, and later academic research.

vocabulary.definition: the main point an informational text develops
an extra component, route, or method that can take over if another fails
how consistently a system works as intended
a place where one failure could stop the whole system
a benefit gained while accepting a cost or disadvantage
a detail that explains or proves the central idea

lessons.written_instruction: Read for the central idea, not just individual examples. After citing evidence, explain what the detail proves.

worked_examples.title: Evidence and significance
worked_examples.solution: A hospital may have backup electrical power.
worked_examples.explanation: If normal power fails, critical equipment can continue; the backup reduces one failure point.

independent_practice.prompt: State the TOPIC in 2-5 words.
State the CENTRAL IDEA in one complete sentence.
Define redundancy using the article.
Give TWO examples of redundancy from the article.
Explain how multiple safe exits reduce a single failure point.
Why does the author discuss costs and maintenance?
What trade-off does a designer consider when adding redundancy?
Write a 3-sentence objective summary.

exit_ticket.prompt: Choose one detail from the article and explain exactly how it supports the central idea.
exit_ticket.answer: Open response with accurate evidence and significance.

exit_ticket.prompt: TEST: Define redundancy.
exit_ticket.answer: An extra component, route, or method that can take over if another fails.

exit_ticket.prompt: TEST: Give one example of redundancy and explain why it can improve reliability.
exit_ticket.answer: Open response with example and reasoning.

lessons.voice_prompt: Do not give the central idea before Atticus reads. After he cites evidence, ask What does that prove? Keep replies short. Do not give assigned answers. For test- items, no hints, confirmation, teaching, or answers until the test is submitted.

lessons.subject: writing
lessons.previous_learning: September 9 writing showed good selection of two different examples, with continued need to make reasoning explicit and avoid repetition.
lessons.course_context: Strengthen claim-evidence-reasoning structure using the informational reading from the same day.
learning_objectives: Write a clear claim.
Use two different evidence examples.
Explain why each example supports the claim.
Include a trade-off and conclusion without repetition.
lessons.why_it_matters: Academic writing is strongest when every detail has a clear purpose in the explanation.

vocabulary.definition: the main explanation being made
a specific detail supporting the explanation
why the evidence supports the claim
evidence followed by reasoning
a word or phrase connecting ideas
restating the same point without adding information

lessons.written_instruction: Plan claim, evidence 1, reasoning 1, evidence 2, reasoning 2, trade-off, and conclusion. Each sentence should add new information.

worked_examples.title: Evidence chain 1
worked_examples.solution: If one exit is blocked, people can use another route.
worked_examples.explanation: The backup route reduces the chance that one failure stops evacuation.

worked_examples.title: Evidence chain 2
worked_examples.solution: Critical equipment can continue if normal power fails.
worked_examples.explanation: The backup protects an important function when the primary system fails.

independent_practice.prompt: Write a clear claim: Why can redundancy improve reliability?
Choose one exact detail from the article for Evidence 1.
Write reasoning explaining why Evidence 1 supports your claim.
Choose a DIFFERENT detail for Evidence 2.
Write reasoning explaining why Evidence 2 supports your claim.

Write 8-10 sentences explaining why redundancy can improve reliability. Include a claim, TWO different examples, reasoning after each example, one trade-off, and a conclusion. Do not repeat the same idea in different words.

exit_ticket.prompt: TEST: Write 5-6 sentences explaining why planning for failure can make a system stronger. Include one piece of evidence and reasoning.
exit_ticket.answer: Open response scored for claim, evidence, reasoning, and conclusion.

lessons.voice_prompt: Do not dictate sentences. If reasoning repeats evidence, say only: That repeats the detail. Tell me why it matters. Address one issue at a time. For test- items, no hints, sentence suggestions, confirmation, or content help until the test is submitted.
